chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa from al-Hasan ibn al-Jahm from Thal'abah from Abd al-Malik ibn Utbah said:

I asked some of these, meaning Abu Yusuf and Abu Hanifa, and I said: 'I constantly hand over money as muḍārabah (profit-sharing partnership) to a man, and he says: It has been lost or gone.' He said: 'Then hand over most of it to him as a loan (qarḍ), and the remainder as muḍārabah.' I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about that, and he said: 'It is permissible.'

key_terms.أَبُو حَنِيفَةَ: Abu Hanifa, the founder of the Hanafi school
key_terms.أَبُو يُوسُفَ: Abu Yusuf, a prominent Hanafi jurist
key_terms.قَرْضًا: Loan, specifically an interest-free loan used here to secure capital
key_terms.مُضَارَبَة: Profit-sharing partnership where one party provides capital and the other labor

ai.seo_question: How to protect investment capital in a muḍārabah partnership if the partner claims loss?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* highlights a pragmatic legal mechanism in Shia jurisprudence to mitigate the risk of capital loss in *muḍārabah* when the partner claims insolvency. By converting the majority of funds into a secured loan (*qarḍ*) while retaining a portion as active partnership capital, the investor balances security with potential profit. Imam al-Sadiq’s validation of this mixed structure underscores the flexibility of Shia commercial law in addressing real-world financial uncertainties.
